the bacterial community of a site affected by human activity is characterized by a high proportion of 16S RNA gene sequences belonging to microflora typically present in soil and freshwater and that the addition of crude oil rapidly induces a shift in the bacterial community with an increase of gamma-Proteo bacteria.

the addition of crude oil induced a rapid shift in the composition and structure of bacterial communities of the coastal seawater of the Rod Bay, and that the oil enrichment culture yielded a number of novel, cold-adaptation hydrocarbonoclastic bacterial strains with potential for industrial applications.
the addition of crude oil induced a shift in bacterial communities from a typical soil and freshwater community to a typical marine community.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the characterization of the microbial communities of the coastal Antarctic marine environment in relation to human activities, and the isolation and screening of hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria with biotechnological potential.

the identification of novel cold-adapted bacterial strains with biotechnological potential and with the assessment of the impact of human activities on the coastal microbial communities of Terra Nova Bay, a pristine area of the Ross Sea, Antarctica.
the identification of bacterial strains that are able to survive in the Antarctic marine environment and to degrade hydrocarbons under low temperature conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Rod Bay site is more polluted than the Adelie cove site, and that this is reflected by the bacterial community structure.
crude oil contamination induces a shift in the structure and composition of the microbial community of the Antarctic marine coastal waters, with the appearance of novel bacterial taxa.

the bacterial community of Rod Bay is characterized by the presence of taxa that are typical of soil, freshwater, and marine environments, whereas the bacterial community of Adelie Cove is dominated by taxa that are typically found in the marine environments affected by algal bloom and sea-ice decay.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the addition of crude oil induced a significant shift in the structure of the bacterial community of Rod Bay seawater, which was characterized by the appearance of novel taxonomical groups and the increase in the abundance of gamma-Proetobacteria.
the bacterial community in the Rod Bay sample was affected by crude oil addition, whereas no significant effect was detected for the Adelie Bay sample.

the microbial community of Rod Bay is characterized by a high diversity of bacterial taxa, including some that have never before been reported in Antarctic coastal waters, and that crude oil addition to this community induces rapid and dramatic changes in its composition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of crude oil rapidly and dramatically changed the composition of the indigenous bacterial community of the Rod Bay site.
the addition of crude oil induced a shift in bacterial composition in the Rod Bay seawaters, with a dramatic increase in gamma-Proteobacterial sequences.

the addition of a small amount of crude oil to coastal seawater in the Terra Nova bay induced a rapid shift in the composition and abundance of the resident bacterial community, which was characterized by the presence of novel taxonomic group and an increase in the abundance of gamma-Proetobacteria sequences.
